claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native, thin passive iron-oxide film.
The native oxide film is composed largely of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
As-received Q235 steel contains microstructural heterogeneities such as grain boundaries and inclusions.
The structure and integrity of the native oxide film govern the corrosion behavior of pre-exposure Q235 steel.
At room temperature in harsh chloride-rich environments, the native oxide film remains intact and suppresses further corrosion.
Elevated temperature accelerates diffusion and oxidation kinetics in the surface film.
Accelerated high-temperature oxidation causes oxide-film thickening and increased defect formation.
Elevated-temperature oxide-film defects include microcracks and oxygen vacancies.
Microcracks and oxygen vacancies act as preferential sites for localized corrosion initiation.
Thermally induced film changes destabilize the passive layer and cause localized corrosion breakdown at elevated temperature.
Controlled thermal conditioning can produce a more uniform, adherent, and protective oxide film on Q235 steel.
A uniform and adherent preconditioned oxide layer can suppress corrosion degradation at elevated temperature.
At elevated temperature, thermally conditioned samples will have lower mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
At elevated temperature, thermally conditioned samples will develop fewer corrosion pits than untreated Q235 steel.
After elevated-temperature exposure, thermally conditioned samples will retain a more uniform passive film than untreated Q235 steel.
At room temperature, both treated and untreated samples will exhibit relatively low corrosion rates.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to controlled chloride-containing aqueous exposures lasting up to approximately 100 hours.
